meta.title: Canadian Cyber Incident Cost Simulator — CA-2026
meta.description: Estimate the financial exposure of a cyber incident in Canada: technical response, legal and regulatory costs, business impact and insurance, by province — with a simulated range of outcomes.

header.title: Cyber Incident
header.subtitle: Visualizing the financial and operational gravity of a cyber incident through a Canadian lens — grounded in provincial regulatory frameworks, published breach cost research, and legal precedent.

In reality those either happen or they don't, and effort, downtime and amounts vary. Each simulated incident draws them at random; the curve shows how often the loss exceeds a given amount.

cards.churnText: Customer churn varies by industry and public perception. For Canadian SMBs, a significant breach often correlates with 15–20% revenue contraction in the following fiscal year. Reputational damage to enterprise organizations can persist 3–5 years.
cards.onePercent: For scale: every 1% of annual revenue lost to churn or contraction costs about {amount} per year.

timeline.title: Cost Timeline
timeline.subtitle: When breach costs actually land
timeline.aria: Cumulative cost timeline: Year 1 {year1}, Year 2+ {year2}, total by month 36 {total}, followed by Variable X, which is not quantified.
timeline.year1Desc: — incident response, forensics, IT restoration, breach counsel, notification & credit monitoring, operational losses, ransom, and insurance premium impact.
timeline.year2Desc: — regulatory fines, commissioner penalties, class-action settlements and defence, which typically resolve well after the initial incident.
timeline.varXDesc: — open-ended: customer churn, revenue contraction, and reputational damage that can compound for 3–5 years. Shown without a dollar value on purpose.

notices.QC: **REGULATORY NOTICE — Loi 25 (QC):** Severe penalties apply. Penal fines can reach **$25M or 4% of worldwide turnover** (whichever is greater). The CAI and affected individuals must be notified promptly where there is a risk of serious injury.
notices.ON: **REGULATORY NOTICE — PIPEDA + PHIPA (ON):** If PHI is involved, PHIPA applies: administrative penalties up to **$500,000** and offence fines up to **$1,000,000** for organizations. Class-action risk is the primary financial driver in Ontario.
notices.AB: **REGULATORY NOTICE — PIPA (AB):** Notification required when there is a real risk of significant harm. Fines are statutory but low; focus is on cause remediation.
notices.BC: **REGULATORY NOTICE — PIPA (BC):** Similar to Alberta. Recent case law strengthens “Intrusion upon Seclusion” tort claims.
notices.OTHER: **REGULATORY NOTICE — PIPEDA (Federal):** Mandatory breach reporting to the OPC when there is a Real Risk of Significant Harm (RROSH). Non-compliance is a serious offence.
notices.FED: **REGULATORY NOTICE — PIPEDA (Federal):** Mandatory breach reporting to the OPC when there is a Real Risk of Significant Harm (RROSH). Non-compliance is a serious offence.
notices.FIN: **REGULATORY NOTICE — PIPEDA + OSFI B-13:** Federally regulated financial entities must comply with OSFI B-13. Failures trigger supervisory intervention and increased capital requirements.
notices.QC_PUB: **REGULATORY NOTICE — Quebec public bodies:** Under the public-sector access and privacy act and the Regulation respecting confidentiality incidents, an incident that presents a **risk of serious injury** must be reported to the CAI and to the persons concerned, and every incident must be recorded in a register.
notices.ON_PUB: **REGULATORY NOTICE — FIPPA / MFIPPA (ON):** Since **July 1, 2025**, provincial institutions must report breaches that pose a real risk of significant harm to the IPC, notify affected individuals as soon as feasible and file an annual breach report. Municipal institutions (MFIPPA) have no explicit duty, though the IPC recommends notification. Hospitals and other health information custodians also fall under PHIPA.
notices.AB_PUB: **REGULATORY NOTICE — POPA (AB):** Since **June 11, 2025**, the Protection of Privacy Act replaces FOIP's privacy rules for public bodies and requires breach notification where there is a real risk of significant harm.
notices.BC_PUB: **REGULATORY NOTICE — FIPPA (BC):** Since **February 1, 2023**, public bodies must notify affected individuals and the Commissioner without undue delay when a breach could reasonably be expected to result in significant harm.
notices.OTHER_PUB: **REGULATORY NOTICE — provincial / territorial public-sector law:** Breach notification duties for public bodies vary by jurisdiction; check the applicable access and privacy act.
notices.FED_PUB: **REGULATORY NOTICE — Privacy Act (federal institutions):** Material privacy breaches must be reported to the OPC and the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat under the TBS Policy on Privacy Protection.

ncta.title: CCCS NATIONAL CYBER THREAT ASSESSMENT 2025–2026
ncta.meta: Published October 30, 2024 by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
ncta.intro: Key findings of the Cyber Centre's assessment of the threats Canada faces in 2025–2026:

trends.label: Ransomware
trends.body: The top cybercrime threat to Canada's critical infrastructure.

trends.label: Cybercrime-as-a-Service
trends.body: Keeps cybercrime persistent, widespread and resilient to disruption.

trends.label: State Actors
trends.body: More aggressive, pairing disruptive attacks with online information campaigns. The PRC runs the most sophisticated and active program targeting Canada; Russia seeks to destabilise Canada and its allies; Iran uses cyber operations to coerce and harass opponents.

trends.label: Non-State Groups
trends.body: Geopolitical tensions are inspiring activity from non-state groups.

ncta.alert: **IBM 2025 (Canada):** average breach cost **CA$6.98M**, up 10.4% from CA$6.32M; financial sector **CA$9.97M**, industrial CA$8.39M, pharmaceutical CA$7.99M. **Sophos 2025 (17 countries):** median ransom payment **US$1M**, down from US$2M; 53% of victims fully recovered within a week.

disclaimer: This simulator produces illustrative estimates based on Canadian industry averages, published breach cost research, and legal precedent. The headline figure is a point estimate; the simulated range shows the spread of plausible outcomes. This tool does not constitute legal, actuarial, or financial advice. Consult qualified counsel before making risk management or insurance decisions.

assumptions.title: Model assumptions & sources
assumptions.intro: Every figure the simulator uses comes from data/model.json. Values tagged “Author estimate” have no external citation; values that also cite a source were calibrated against it.
rules: Size: response effort, counsel hours, remediation and ransom amounts are interpolated between four size anchors on a log scale, using headcount when given and annual revenue otherwise.

Operations disruption = annual revenue ÷ 365 × days of disruption × share of operations affected × industry revenue at risk × (1 + extra operating cost). It cannot exceed what the organisation would have earned during the outage, plus that extra cost.

Notification, credit monitoring, regulatory fines and the class-action reserve only apply when personal information is exposed: always for data breaches and insider incidents, for ransomware only when exfiltration occurred, for BEC only when mailbox personal information was accessed, never for DDoS.
Public bodies are assessed under public-sector privacy law; no monetary penalty is modelled for them.

Point estimate: every driver at its most likely value, fines and class actions counted at amount × probability. The simulated range draws each driver from a triangular distribution and each fine or class action as an event.

Insurance: the deductible sits inside the limit; business interruption during the waiting period is not covered; ransomware claims are capped by the sublimit and reduced by coinsurance; the 3-year premium increase only applies when a claim is paid. Net = gross − covered + premium increase.
Severity compares the headline exposure (net of insurance when a policy is entered) with annual revenue. Variable X (brand & reputation) is described but not given a dollar value.

params.itHoursPerIrHour: IT recovery hours per IR hour
params.unpaidDowntimeMult: Disruption if the ransom is not paid
params.unpaidItRecoveryMult: IT rebuild effort if the ransom is not paid
params.becRecoveredShareIfReportedFast: BEC funds recovered when reported within 24 h
params.extraCostRate: Extra operating cost during disruption (share of lost revenue)
params.premiumRateOfLimit: Annual premium when not entered (share of limit)

cols.extortion: Ransom / fraud loss at each anchor

assumptions.fineRevenuePct: {pct} of revenue ({pctPhi} with PHI), capped at max({cap}, {capPct} of revenue)
assumptions.fedRule: Private sector: federal entities in finance or telecom use the PIPEDA + OSFI B-13 regime. Public bodies use the public-sector regime of their jurisdiction.

methodology.title: Methodology & Sources
methodology.intro: How the simulator turns a scenario into a cost estimate, every parameter it uses, and where each one comes from. Everything below is generated from the same data/model.json the simulator reads.

formulas.name: Gross exposure
formulas.text: Technical response + Legal, regulatory & settlements + Business impact

formulas.name: Technical response
formulas.text: IR hours × (IR rate × IR multiplier + forensic ratio × forensic rate × forensic multiplier + IT ratio × IT rate), where IR hours = incident IR hours × size effort × control factors

formulas.name: Business impact
formulas.text: Operations disruption (revenue-based, see below) + remediation + ransom or fraud loss

formulas.name: Legal
formulas.text: Counsel + (if personal data exposed) notification + double-extortion surcharge + credit monitoring + fine + settlement + defence, with fine, settlement and defence weighted by probability in the point estimate

formulas.name: Insurance
formulas.text: Covered = max(0, min(gross − uncovered waiting period, cap) − deductible) × (1 − coinsurance); Net = gross − covered + premium increase

calibration: Settlements: Desjardins (2022) — up to $200.85M for about 9.7M people, roughly $21 per affected person including five years of credit monitoring. LifeLabs (2023) — up to $9.8M for about 8.6M people, roughly $1 per affected person. The model's base and finance premium sit near Desjardins; the simulated range reaches down to LifeLabs.

Ransomware: Sophos 2025 reports a median ransom payment of US$1M (down from US$2M), median demands under US$350K for organisations with revenue of US$250M or less, and 53% of victims fully recovered within a week. Ransom amounts and the 10-day disruption are calibrated to that.
Benchmark: IBM 2025 puts the average Canadian breach at CA$6.98M; organisations using security AI and automation extensively averaged CA$5.19M versus CA$8.53M without.
